opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the underappreciated bottlenecks. When people talk about AI for science, they tend to picture the model doing the thinking: proposing hypotheses, designing experiments. But a lot of the leverage actually comes from the other side, which is how much signal you can get out of the physical world and how fast.

In domains like language or code, the data is already digital. It's sitting there, and you can scrape it, verify it, and iterate in a tight loop. In materials science or biology you don't have that. The world is mostly unmeasured. A cell is doing an enormous amount of computation, and we're looking at it through a keyhole: a few readouts, a few markers, some imaging at a particular resolution. So the question becomes: what are the sensors, and what is the throughput of the loop from "the model has an idea" to "we got a measurement back"?

I'd break it down into a few things. One is bandwidth. How many dimensions are you actually observing? Something like single-cell sequencing or high-content imaging gives you far richer information per experiment than a single scalar assay. Two is throughput and cost. Can you run thousands or millions of these cheaply, with automation and robotics, so the model gets enough examples to learn from? Three is fidelity and reproducibility. Noisy, inconsistent measurements are basically poison for training, and lab-to-lab variation is a real problem.

So my mental model is that you want to turn the lab into something that looks more like a data engine: highly instrumented, automated, with standardized readouts that feed straight back into the model. Whoever builds that closed loop, rather than just training a model on whatever papers exist, is probably going to have a big advantage. In a lot of these fields the models are in some sense ahead of the sensors right now, and that's where I'd expect a lot of interesting work to happen.

r001.rationale: The response frames sensors and lab instrumentation as the way AI receives measurements from the physical world, citing single-cell sequencing and high-content imaging as examples.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the places where my mental model of AI progress diverges a bit from the default narrative. The default narrative is something like: you build a sufficiently smart model, you ask it to cure cancer or discover a room-temperature superconductor, and it just goes off and does it. And I think that's just not how it works, because the bottleneck in a lot of these fields was never really the thinking. It was the measuring.

If you look at what actually drove progress in materials science or biology historically, it's instruments. The microscope, X-ray crystallography, sequencing, cryo-EM. Each of those basically opened up a new channel of information from the physical world into the scientific process. And the thinking part, the hypothesis part, was often kind of downstream of that. You see something new and then you reason about it.

So when I think about AI-driven research, I think the AI is sort of a very capable brain in a jar right now. It has read everything, it can reason, but it has very impoverished senses. It can't poke at the world. And the question is what does the sensory and motor system look like that you attach to it. And I think it ends up looking like automated labs, where you have robotic pipetting, imaging, spectroscopy, all of it instrumented and streaming data in a format that the model can consume directly, and the model is in a loop where it proposes an experiment, the lab runs it, the data comes back, and it updates.

The thing I'd emphasize is that the sensors matter more than people think because the model is only as good as the data distribution it's trained on and conditioned on. A lot of biology is tacit. It lives in the hands of the grad student who knows the cells look a little off today. That information never makes it into a paper, so the model never sees it. If you want the model to actually do biology, you have to capture that. High-throughput imaging, continuous monitoring, logging everything, not just the summary statistic that goes into the figure. In some sense you want to build the lab as a data-generating process for the model, rather than a place where humans do experiments and occasionally write things down.

And then I think there's a flywheel there that's really interesting. Once the loop is closed, the model can start to ask for the measurements it needs. It can say, this is the ambiguity in my current understanding, this is the experiment that would resolve it. And that's a very different regime from what we have today, where the model is basically a very well-read consultant that you talk to but that has never actually touched a pipette.

So I'd say the sensors are not a detail. They're kind of the whole thing. The intelligence is becoming cheap and abundant, and the scarce resource becomes bits from reality. Whoever builds the best pipes from the physical world into these models is going to be the one who actually gets the scientific progress out of them.

r001.rationale: It describes automated labs and their instruments—such as imaging and spectroscopy—as the sensory system that connects AI to the physical world, explicitly including materials science.

astra-6.text:
I think about it in terms of the loop you’re trying to close. What can the AI observe, what experiments can it propose, and how does it get feedback? A lot of the excitement is around the intelligence in the middle, but that intelligence needs some way to interact with the thing you’re studying.

In materials science and biology, you don’t get to observe the entire state of the system. You have measurements, and each measurement gives you a particular view. So the question is whether those observations are sufficient to distinguish your hypotheses. If two explanations predict exactly the same thing in everything you can measure, then more thinking alone may not help. You need a different experiment or a different measurement.

And I’d want the AI to participate in that choice. Given what it currently believes, what should it measure next? What would reduce uncertainty the most, relative to the time and cost? Then you’re building a loop where the model proposes an experiment, instruments collect the result, and the model updates its understanding. The sensors and the ability to run experiments are a pretty fundamental part of that system.

r001.rationale: The response describes sensors and instruments as the means for observing the system and collecting experimental results, identifying their role as the AI’s interface to the research subject.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as closing the loop. You can have a model that reads all the papers and proposes experiments, but at some point it needs to take an action in the physical world and observe what happened. The sensors are how you get that observation back into the system.

And the interesting question is whether the observation tells you enough. If you’re trying to make a material with some property, can you measure that property reliably? How long does it take? How expensive is it? In biology, you might have a measurement that’s very easy to collect but only indirectly related to the thing you actually care about. Then the AI can get very good at optimizing that measurement without solving your problem.

So I’d think about the whole experimental loop: what can you manipulate, what can you observe, and how quickly can you repeat it? Better models help, but if every experiment takes a month and the feedback is ambiguous, that’s a pretty fundamental bottleneck. The exciting setup is one where you can automate the experiment, get informative feedback, and let the system use that feedback to choose the next experiment.

r001.rationale: The response explains that sensors return observations to the AI during experiments, but it does not identify laboratory equipment as the sensory interface.
